utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Mr. Tieger, I'm not sure whether he was introduced before or not. Could you introduce your colleague again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Seated to my immediate right is Mr. Amir Zec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Before we start hearing the next witness today, I have a few procedural matters to address. First, in order to ensure that the trial is conducted expeditiously, the Chamber monitors the pace of the proceedings on an ongoing basis using the time statistics provided by the Registry. At the end of July 2011, the Prosecution has used more than 160 hours of the 300 hours allocated for the presentation of its case. From the courtesy copy of the tentative list of witnesses who remain to be called by -- by the Prosecution, which was communicated yesterday, the Chamber observes that the Prosecution has called 93 witnesses in addition to one Chamber witness thus far and intends to call an additional 118 witnesses. At this stage, the Chamber would, therefore, like the Prosecution to address, in writing and by close of business on 26 August 2011, how it foresees that it will be able to call its total number of witnesses while keeping within the 300-hour limit imposed at the beginning of trial. Second, the Chamber refers to the Prosecution motion for leave to amend its witness and exhibit list filed confidentially on 21st of July, 2011 and associated filings. The Chamber requires the Prosecution, by close of business on 26 August 2011, again, to file confidentially a further written submission which outlines: One, why there is good cause for the addition of KDZ-600 at this stage of the proceedings. In answering that question, the Prosecution should identify whether or not there are other witnesses who are ready -- who are already on the witness list who will be testifying about the same or similar events and why KDZ-600's proposed testimony is considered unique. Number two, explain in more detail how the unfolding of the accused's case suddenly promoted the Prosecution to consider calling KDZ-600 as a witness and whether the relevance of her evidence only recently became apparent. I should have said prompted instead of promoted. Third, the Chamber will now issue an oral ruling with regard to the accused's motion for reclassification of ex parte appendix KDZ-490 and KDZ-492 protective measures, filed on 22nd August, 2011. The Chamber notes the Prosecution's response filed yesterday, not opposing the motion. The Chamber hereby grants the motion and orders that the confidential and ex parte appendix to the Prosecution's response to Karadzic's motion for modification of delayed disclosure, Witness KDZ-490 and KDZ-492 filed on 9th of March, 2010 be disclosed to the accused and reclassified as confidential. Finally, the accused's request not on sit on Monday is denied, and the hearing will therefore proceed on Monday morning as scheduled. Unless there are any matters to be raised, we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, with leave I have a correction to the exhibit list. On 22nd August 2011 65 ter 90253 was admitted as Exhibit P3183 under seal. The Registry would correct this exhibit number to read as Exhibit P3195 under seal. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. President, is Dzevad Gusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance, Your Excellencies, concerning the number of witnesses? I believe the Prosecution has a problem. They don't have a case. That's why they're trying to snow me under quantity instead of quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is an utterly improper comment at the moment. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gusic. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, can we begin by having you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dzevad Gusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gusic, is it correct that you provided statements to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 15th of February, 1999, and also on the 2nd of May, 2003, and that you also testified before this Tribunal on the 5th and 6th of May, 2003, in that instance in the case of Prosecutor v. Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: All that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gusic, are you also aware that a statement, a so-called amalgamated statement, containing portions of your previous testimony and statements has been assembled and is reflected in 65 ter 90264?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps we could call that up.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It appears that the document's not released, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, the question was simply whether you were aware that an amalgamated statement containing portions of your previous testimony and statements was prepared.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, have you had the opportunity to review your previous statements and your testimony in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I have. I have had the opportunity to review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And have you also had the opportunity to review the amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I have had the opportunity to review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that you wish to make certain clarifications to the statement. Let me address those quickly. First of all, your statement refers to 65 ter 11734, which is essentially a resume or CV. Perhaps it would be useful to update that, and if you could simply tell the Chamber quickly what you are doing -- what your work is now.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I'm currently working as chef de cabinet of the deputy state secretary for finance of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 3 of your amalgamated statement, paragraph 5, it states that up until the 2 of March, 1992, that the SDA president was Mirsad Kavazbasic. I understand you wanted to change -- clarify that date from the 2nd of March to another date?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: That's right. Some mistake must have occurred. It was not the 2nd of March but the 20th of March, 1992. That's when I became president of the SDA for Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. That appears to be a simple typo since there's at least one other reference in your statement to that time period that is consistent with what you've just said. I also wanted to direct your attention to paragraph 12, which is on page 9, which is a continuation of something you said at page 8. There you refer to something that you were told by an official of the SDA, who said to you that Karadzic on one occasion had said to him words to the effect, "We'll have to split up. There's no other way. That will be the best thing." And you identified that person at page 9 as Osman Brka. And I understand that your clarification has to do with a subsequent discussion you had after your testimony in the Milosevic case about whether Mr. Brka was -- had any doubts that he was speaking to Mr. Karadzic or someone else at that time.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: After I testified in the Milosevic case, I had occasion to speak again to Mr. Brka, and I told him that in my evidence and in my statements I provided the information that we had discussed at one point, namely that he had spoken to Radovan Karadzic, and when Karadzic said that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be divided, he said he couldn't really remember that it was Karadzic. It may have been another official. He did not sound very confident, so I'm saying this because I feel it's necessary to make a correction there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Gusic. Next I wanted to direct your attention to page 25, paragraph 42. Your statement says there, and that's taken from the 1999 ICTY statement: "It was amazing that during these times every local Serb, without exception, changed overnight into having a total dislike for Muslims." And I understand you wanted to clarify that, Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I wanted to make it clearer, make a small correction. When I made that statement in 1999, I believe that through a combination of circumstances it was not recorded very precisely. It cannot be said that every Serb hated Muslims. Rather, the case was that the general attitude of Serbs towards Muslims has changed, and some Serbs individually had a strong hatred towards Muslims that they did not even bother to hide. So it was the general attitude of Serbs that changed. The Serbs were obsessed the policy of Greater Serbia and in speaking with their Muslim neighbours, they always emphasised that Serbs were a great people, a great nation, that it has to be the leading nation in the state, that they must have a large state like Russia, that they have Slobodan Milosevic and his Yugoslav People's Army who will protect them, that they all must live in one state. And in these discussions when one of their peers wanted to put to them counter-arguments, namely that what they were saying was a nationalist idea, that it would lead to nothing good, that there would be a rise in ethnic tensions, that there would be a rift between peoples and hatred, whatever a Bosniak would put to them such arguments, the Serbs would label him as an enemy of the Serb people and would view him with mistrust and misgivings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Next I wanted to turn your attention to page 39 of the amalgamated statement, which is part of a paragraph 73, which is a long paragraph. At the bottom of page 39 you were asked about certain period, and you said: "Well, this was carried out --" that is the period of mid -- or mid-1992, in that case July 1992, and you said: "Well, this was carried out when the occupation of Bratunac was carried out, when the ethnic cleansing of villages was carried out and when thousands of civilians were killed, thousands of Muslim civilians in Bratunac." And I wanted to ask you in connection with your clarifications whether the term "thousands" was literally true and what figure you considered accurate and how you came to an understanding of that figure.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, the total of Muslims killed in Bratunac was 3.500 in less than two months. Foreign military units from Serbia and local police forces -- I mean Serb police forces in Bratunac killed about 1.000 Muslim civilians in less than one month, including women, the elderly, the infirm, children. That figure is not final. According to information available currently, the total of civilian fatalities in the first months of war, and that means that we have exact personal details of each victim, is 670 casualties of war against -- amongst civilians. That is not a final figure, as I said. There are many families who are still searching for their near and dear and their bodies, and there are also many people not from Bratunac who happened to be in Bratunac at the time on whom we don't have complete information. So it's only an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. And two more quick corrections that appear to be typos. First, paragraph 73, page 37. You are recorded as stating: "I think that as regards -- I think that as regards those activities it's not even worth mentioning in view of the fact that Bratunac was a peaceful place, calm place, by offered in resistance on the 17th of April." And I understand you wanted to change something that seems apparent, "that offered no resistance on the 17th of April." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, 1992, foreign military units from Serbia entered Bratunac and together with local military and police forces and the Territorial Defence, they occupied Bratunac, took over the government and the power in Bratunac without a single gunshot fired and started ethnic cleansing and killings. But on the 17th of April, 1992, not a single Bosniak fired a single bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally at page 44, paragraph 77, again it's obviously a typo, I think. There's a reference to a question about roadblocks in the village of Glogova and here it says Branca and Pervani, and I understand that instead of Branca it should say Hranca.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: It should be H-r-a-n-c-a, Hranca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. And with those clarifications, can you confirm that the amalgamated statement accurately reflects your prior statements, that those statements were accurate and truthful and that if asked about the same issues you would provide the same information here in court?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: The amalgamated statement is accurate, and even if I had to make a new one before the Court today, I would give the same statement. I would probably not be able to formulate everything in the same words, but the essence would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender 90264, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I would ask that paragraph 12, which repeats the version of contact with Dr. Karadzic by Osman Brka be stricken from the amalgamated statement. First of all, I want to thank the witness for making that clarification. I think that's very commendable that he did that. And now that it's in that state, it has absolutely no probative value. It's completely -- it's double hearsay, something Osman Brka told him, and the second part of the hearsay is completely unsourced because we don't know who it was who made that statement. I realise hearsay is admissible, but there's a limit to it and I think this exceeds that limit. So I would ask that paragraph 12 just be deleted from the amalgamated statement and it be admitted without that issue being part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I hear from you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I agree with and appreciate Mr. Robinson's compliments to the witness, but would I say that, first of all, this has been adequately clarified by the correction, and it continues to have some utility to the Court, because the information in its totality now is that a SDA official at the time had a discussion with an SDS official. I think -- I see the Court nodding. I see you take my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to reply, Mr. Robinson. With such clarification, there should be no harm to the accused, no prejudice, because it may be another official. Why do we have to strike out?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because it would be completely unsafe for you to use that for any purpose at this trial. How can we confront that, an unnamed SDS official making some statement? If you gave it any weight whatsoever I think it would be completely unsafe. And when you have something that has no probative value, zero, then I think you should exclude it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think we need to dwell on this too much. It doesn't no probative value. There's considerable evidence in the case elsewhere about calls for division. This is one more element which the court can consider in its assessment of the climate at the time and the positions taken by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the -- the Chamber would like some assistance. Now, we have evidence from the witness quite clearly that Brka is now saying that he was not sure that it was Karadzic. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Well, could one say that the entire foundation by this revelation has been shaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I wouldn't look at it that way, Your Honour. I would look at it in the following fashion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- and that is the witness had a conversation with a particular person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- who related in -- a discussion that person had both about content and about the identity of the participant. In a subsequent discussion, that source didn't recant the content but just expressed doubt about the specific source of the information as being Dr. Karadzic in contrast to any other SDS -- to another SDS official. So I would say, in fact, that the foundation to a certain -- to a large extent was supported and confirmed and to another -- on another matter very specific aspect of what was related then was undercut. That's what the witness told us about. So there are various elements, as I understand it, to that previous discussion. The source of that information confirmed what I would say was the bulk of it, but also gave cause to doubt that the specific source of that information was a particular SDS official, that is, Dr. Karadzic. So I would say you have a considerable degree of confirmation and some degree of undeniable doubt about the -- about whether it was Dr. Karadzic in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Robinson, we should like very much to hear you in rely to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Judge Baird. Think about this: Would you admit a statement -- I don't think even the Prosecution would offer this, but if they did, some witness came and said, "I was told by a friend of mine that he had a conversation with an unknown or unnamed SDS official, we don't know when it took place, we don't know where it took place we don't know who else was present, we don't know the context, but here is what was said." I don't think that would even be offered in such a trial, let alone that you would admit such evidence. And certainly it would be unfair to rely on it in any way whatsoever in your judgement. So I think this is the same situation. The witness gave some evidence that at one time had probative value because the speaker was identified as President Karadzic. It's no longer that situation. Now examining the new situation, it's clearly an inadmissible hearsay that is so far removed and so unreliable that it shouldn't even be considered by the Chamber and given any weight, and when something has no probative value, then it shouldn't be admitted in the first place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll stop here. Usually the Chamber is not involved in the business of analysing the probative value in the middle of -- middle of a hearing and strike some part of evidence. Let me consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will issue a ruling in relation to the request from the -- from the accused to strike this part, i.e., para 12. Subject to that, this statement will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- particularly in light of the Court's awareness of overlooking a summary previously, I will now read with the Court's permission a summary of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's important for the purpose of the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gusic, as indicated, this is simply a brief summary of your evidence. It doesn't purport to be evidence itself. It's the statement that you provided. Nor does it presume to attempt to cover everything you said. And now the summary. Following the multi-party elections in 1990, the witness was a member of the Municipal Assembly on behalf of the SDA in Bratunac municipality from approximately March 20th, 1992, to 17 April 1992. He served as president of the SDA in Bratunac following the departure of the then president. In those capacities, the witness met and dealt with various SDS political figures in Bratunac, including the president of the SDS in Bratunac, Miroslav Deronjic. Although it had won more than 50 per cent of the vote in Bratunac, the SDA agreed to SDS demands for a two-thirds majority requirement for decisions in the Assembly, which gave the SDS greater control in the Assembly than its electoral numbers, and also agreed to a 50/50 power-sharing arrangement. The SDA accepted the 50/50 principle in order to avoid blockade of the work in the Assembly. During 1991 as Serb delegates in the republic Assembly were purportedly demanding division of Bosnia, the SDS in Bratunac was establishing parallel structures, including a Crisis Staff, a separate Assembly, and a separate Serb municipality. At the same time, Serbian nationalist attitudes and actions began to increase and be more visible. The witness also received information that the SDS and the JNA were involved in arming and training of local Serb civilians. Additionally, the witness observed that the JNA deployed heavy artillery weapons and mortars at locations around Ljubovija in Serbia, with their barrels pointed toward inhabited settlements in Bratunac. In early April 1992, Miroslav Deronjic and the SDS called a meeting at which he informed the SDA of the SDS intent to divide the police into Muslim and Serb police. Deronjic said that if the -- said that the Serb people felt they were in a minority and unit direct threat from the Muslims and threatened that if the demand was not met, Muslims would disappear. Deronjic said that Radovan Karadzic was placing Deronjic under pressure to get this division underway. Deronjic often spoke of meetings with Karadzic, and the witness understood from him that he was under Karadzic's control. The SDA agreed to these demands in order to maintain the peace and order, and the Serb police was eventually created. On 17 April 1992, the witness received information that some units entered Bratunac, and he observed a military unit stationed around the Fontana Hotel. Later that day, Deronjic told the witness and other SDA officials to attend a meeting in the Fontana Hotel with Deronjic and officers of the Serbian Army. At the meeting, the witness and others were told that Bratunac was a Serb municipality and that Serbian laws would be applied. The witness was told to compile a list of Muslim nationalists. In light of these circumstances and knowing what had happened in other municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, the witness decided to leave the area as soon as possible and managed to do so. He later received information about the fate of Bratunac Muslims, including widespread expulsions, killings, and destruction of mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, although your statement is now in evidence, I have a few additional questions for you that I'd like to ask at this time. First, I noted that at paragraph 14 of your statement, and that's on page 9, you said that: "To illustrate how the climate had changed amongst the people, cafes in Bratunac started to be used for Serb nationalist meetings where Serbs would gather singing Chetnik songs. Posters and slogans began to appear on walls which insulted Muslims and promoted Serb nationalism." You go on to say: "The SDS said that no co-existence was possible and that Bratunac was a Serb municipality." I wanted to ask you if you could just provide any examples and tell the Court what those posters and slogans that began to appear, what kind of things they said.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: After the first multi-party elections were held, the SDS intensified its propaganda, pursuing a policy of a Greater Serbia. That propaganda reached such heights that SDS activists wrote different slogans in different places, highly derogatory as far as Bosniaks were concerned, Muslims as they were called at the time. These slogans were: "This is Serbia, Greater Serbia." "Muslims, Balijas, Turks move out, you're going to be slaughtered." The names of Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic. "There is no Bosnia any more." Then the names of some Chetnik commanders from the Second World War and so on. These slogans were written in streets, on traffic signs, on public buildings, houses, auxiliary buildings, cars, and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your -- your statement reflects, as indicated earlier, the establishment by the SDS of parallel structures in Bosnia, including the demand for division of the police in April into a Muslim and Serb police, and also reflects calls for division of Bosnia more generally at the republic level. I wanted to ask you, before the demand for division of the police in April, had there been discussion by Deronjic or other SDS officials about the ethnic division of Bratunac or -- or the republic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Sometime, perhaps even in the first half of 1991, you could often hear from the political representatives of the Serbs that they wished to live in a Greater Serbia, that Bosnia had to be divided. At the time, we understood this to be mere rhetoric, a wish. We were so naive that we thought this was some kind of fantasy. However, when I took over as president of the SDA for the municipality of Bratunac on the 20th of March, I had several meetings with the president of the SDS of Bratunac, Miroslav Deronjic, and his associates. I was surprised at these meetings. They openly spoke about the division of Bosnia. They proposed that Bosnia be divided. I was taken aback by these ideas. Actually, this idea to divide up Bratunac specifically. I was taken aback by these proposals and ideas, and I asked why would we embark on such a process. Miroslav Deronjic was a very skilful politician. As for extremely nationalist and radical ideas, he knew how to present them as something totally natural, something that should be taken into account. He said quite simply, "You know what? The Serbs need to keep their own Serbdom, their own history, their own tradition, their own culture. They should live separately from the Muslim people if they want to keep all of that. If they want to do that, they can only do it by separating from the Muslim people." That was the first time I took it a bit more seriously. Actually, quite seriously. Then I said to him, "Well, all right. I'm taken aback by these ideas. You cannot do it just off the cuff. There have to be certain plans and projects for implementing such ideas." And he said, "We in the SDS have plans that were prepared. I even have certain instructions how to act with regard to these questions." I suggested something to him, because this was a major idea. I could not decide on this, and I could not state my views in any appropriate manner. I suggested that we bring together some 15 or 20 directors of major companies. Of course, this was a multi-ethnic group. There were Serbs and Muslims there. And then I suggested that he present that idea of his to these directors as well so that we hear their views as well, and he accepted that. He said, "Why not? It should be said. Why would everyone not know that? We're not doing thing surreptitiously." So we organised this meeting there were about 15 or 20 Serbs and Muslims who were directors of major companies, and he said that the Serbs should live separately, that there are plans, that Bratunac should be divided, that Bosnia should be divided and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic, and although this may be corrected in the transcript later I just want to clarify the transcript records you as saying that you said the Serbs need to keep their own Serbdom, their own history. They should live separate from the Muslim people, et cetera. Was that you or was that Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: No. It was Miroslav Deronjic who said that to us, the representatives of the SDA, to us, the Bosniaks, Muslims, as representatives of the municipality. Maybe I was not very specific when speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That may have been just a glitch in the transcript, but it's clear now. Thank you. Mr. Gusic, at page 24 of your statement, you discuss aspects of what you understood about the relationship between Mr. Deronjic and Mr. Karadzic based, in part, on what you heard from Deronjic, including statements that he was under the control of Karadzic, and you indicate that you understood that he was Karadzic's right hand and had wide powers in terms of activity and could invoke Karadzic's name and say Karadzic ordered it if Deronjic couldn't otherwise convince the SDA through his political skills, and I would just ask you to elaborate to the Trial Chamber on what you were trying to convey here about what you understood to be Deronjic's relationship to Karadzic and what it was Deronjic said to you or you otherwise observed that led you to this understanding.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to say that when Miroslav Deronjic was elected president of the SDS in the second half of 1990, the Serbs of Bratunac were saying that there were more deserving candidates and more renowned Serbs than Deronjic. They were saying that some Nikolic should be president of the SDS but that Radovan Karadzic directly intervened and made sure that Miroslav Deronjic would be elected president of the SDS for the municipality of Bratunac. That is what I heard Serbs saying at the time. And we discussed that because we were very interested in who the president of the party would be. Deronjic was a highly disciplined member of the SDS. I'm talking about my own impression now. My impression was that he was very faithful to his president, Radovan Karadzic. He said that Radovan Karadzic had great trust in Miroslav Deronjic. Deronjic was particularly active, and he persisted in having the police in Bratunac divided. We from the SDA did not want to divide the police. We said to him that that would be insane, that dividing the police into a Serb and Muslim police would mean that there would be even more separation between Muslims and Bosniaks and that this would lead to greater tensions and that it would have very bad consequences. He said that he can understand us but that we need to understand him, that he received orders from the top of the SDS signed by his president, Karadzic, and that he had to work on reaching an agreement to divide the police. If we did not agree to this and if we would not divide the police in Bratunac into the Serb police and the Muslim police, he could not guarantee peace and security in that area. He said to us that in Bijeljina the SDA and the SDS did not co-operate well, did not reach proper agreements and foreign military units from Serbia entered the area, occupied Bijeljina, and committed violence in that municipality. He wouldn't want that to happen in Bratunac. He appealed to us saying that we should be reasonable, and we said all right. If we agree to this division of the police, can you guarantee to us that there would be peace and safety in the territory of the municipality of Bratunac and that foreign military forces from Serbia would not enter Bratunac as they entered Bijeljina. He said that if we divide the police, his president, Radovan Karadzic, would be pleased and he would let us continue our discussions, and he guaranteed that we would have peace and security in the municipality of Bratunac, that we should be reasonable and work to that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. In your statement you also describe some of the circumstances extant when you became president of the SDA in March of 1992, including the arming and training of Serbs, the increased tensions and intimidation, the deployment of JNA weaponry, calls for division, and I wanted to ask you if those circumstances caused you concern and if you undertook any efforts to go to Muslim areas or villages to discuss or see about the possibility of defending against attack and, if so, what result?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: When I became president of the SDA for the municipality of Bratunac on the 20th of March, the JNA and the SDS had already armed the Serb people by then. They were saying that they had more weapons, that there were Serbs in Bratunac, and according to the census from 1991, there were 11.500 Serbs in Bratunac. The SDS, on orders from the top leadership of the SDS, illegally established the Serb municipality of Bratunac. Also on orders, they established a war Crisis Staff for the municipality of Bratunac and all the villages in the municipality of Bratunac. We had corroborated information that the JNA and the SDS in certain locations in the municipality of Bratunac were conducting the training of Serb civilians to use weapons and to wage war afterwards. I was so concerned about that, and the first thing I did when I became the president of the SDA was to go and visit some neighbourhoods where there were Muslims as a majority. I wanted to have an open discussion about the complex security situation and the danger of the armed Serb people there and the JNA. I visited several places, and I talked to several activists of the SDA and ordinary citizens. In some of these places -- actually, the first thing I noticed was that the Muslims in these neighbourhoods were terrified. They lived in great fear and uncertainty. They were highly concerned. At some of these places, when I asked about the possibility of us organising ourselves and putting up a resistance if we were to be attacked by Serb forces, if the Serb forces were to attack a particular village or a particular neighbourhood, the answer I would get was that the Muslims of that neighbourhood are honourable and honest people, that they are not to be blamed for anything, that they are not guilty of anything, that they have been living a good life together with their Serb neighbours and that they did not believe that their Serb neighbours would want to deal with them in a brutal way. In some other places, again when I asked that we be organised and put up a resistance if there was an attack, another answer I received was that the Serbs were armed, that they had the JNA that at the time was one of the major armed forces in Europe, and that it was insane to put up any kind of resistance and that putting up a resistance would equal a catastrophe since they had hunting guns and pistols and this is no way to put up a resistance. I notice that had most Muslims in the municipality of Bratunac first of all seemed to believe that there would be no large-scale conflicts, and even if that were to happen, we were on the threshold of the 21st Century and there is an international community. It would intervene very quickly. That was a delusion. I wish to say that during these talks there were certain individuals in all of these neighbourhoods and in all of these villages who had an inkling of what would happen and who insisted that they organise themselves and that they put up a resistance. Therefore, they asked for weapons, and they tried to do something in that way. However, the Serb Democratic Party in the municipality of Bratunac, through their infrastructure and through their war Crisis Staffs for the municipality of Bratunac and for all the villages and through Serb policemen and officials in the municipality of Bratunac they kept Bratunac monitored, closely monitors -- monitored. So all activities in that direction just remained a mere attempt and nothing was actually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. I wanted to now direct your attention to several documents if I may and I'll try to do that as efficiently as possible. First in section with the references today and your amalgamated statement to the establishment of an SDS Crisis Staff in Bratunac, if I could direct your attention quickly to three documents. The first two are -- would be in 65 ter 00590, first at page 83 of the English and page 70 through 71 in the B/C/S. The document doesn't bear a date at the time but it can easily be contextually dated through the reference in the third paragraph to "a meeting held last night, October 18th, 1991, in Sarajevo." And if could I direct your attention, Mr. Gusic, to the next page in -- well -- yeah, that's fine. I think you'll see that there. You'll see a reference to election of the Crisis Staff, and the notation was agreed that only a part of the Crisis Staff should be elected tonight. And then if I could direct your attention next - and as I said I'll show you three documents in connection with this - to page 85 of the English and page 72 of the B/C/S. This is the minutes of a meeting from October 26, 1991, headed "Minutes of the first meeting of the Crisis Staff." And finally if I could direct your attention next to 65 ter 00603, page 8 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S. This is a meeting held on 25 October 1991. And if we see item 3 at the agenda: "Appointment of the Crisis Staff in the Bratunac municipality with the purpose of implementing protective measures for the Serbian people." And if we go quickly to the next page in English and the next page in B/C/S, we see another reference to the Crisis Staff and some of its members. Mr. Gusic, I simply wanted to ask you whether those references are consistent with the information in your amalgamated statement and the statement you provided today about the establishment of an SDS Crisis Staff in the Bratunac municipality in 1991.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would tender the pages containing those particular minutes and meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 00590 will be Exhibit P3197 and 65 ter number 00603 will be Exhibit P3198.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, you referred on a couple of occasions today to the organisation at local levels and information from the local level within Bratunac and within the SDS structure. I just wanted to turn your attention quickly to 65 ter 00590, page 68 of the English and page 58 of the B/C/S. Although this says -- I'm sorry, that's the incorrect reference. My apologies. It should be page 72 of the English and page 61 of the B/C/S. Thank you. And this is a meeting held on March 8th, 1990, although as we'll see from other sessions because it's the 16th session, it appears to be 1991. We'll introduce another session earlier that will indicate that chronology, so I believe that's a typo. We can see it in the -- in the session of the meetings, although I realise it accurately reflects what was written there. In any event, Mr. Gusic, I want to direct your attention to item 1 of the agenda where there's a discussion about the realisation of the elections and mention of the fact that board members would be in charge of running approximately 15 to 20 houses, and then a discussion about the existing local boards and the organisation of citizens. Was that approach to the structure of the SDS, that is members of the local boards being responsible for --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I'm not getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know where the interpretation stopped, Mr. Gusic, but if -- I just wanted to direct your attention to item 1 of the agenda and ask whether the reference to local board members being responsible or in charge of approximately 15 to 20 houses was consistent with your observations and understanding at the time of the organisational level of the SDS in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those pages, Your Honour, 72 through 73 of the English and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that those pages will be added to P3197?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, again you discuss at pages 8 and 9 and discussed again today the establishment of parallel structures in Bratunac in 1991 and 1992. I wanted to direct your attention quickly to 65 ter 00742.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just, in view of the very short time I have for cross-examination, does Mr. Tieger stand by what he said, that his document -- this document is from 1990 or 1991? It's -- it's an important difference, 1990 or 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the -- what we see in the entirety of the collection that is available here is, for example, that the 14th session of the SDS Municipal Board was held on January 22nd 1991. This, the 15th session is then listed as February -- which I will also be turning our attention to, as 15 -- as February 21st, 1990. This one is March 8th, 1990. And we have a reference earlier to the 11th session being held on December 17, 1990. Those are the factors that led me to the comment I made, and at the moment I can offer no more than that. That -- that document is also available to the accused as it was to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that document was disclosed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I note the time. You need some -- how much more would you need to conclude you are in-chief examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if the Court wanted to break now, it wouldn't be -- I think it's probably another ten minutes, I would estimate. Maybe I'm being conservative on that, but I'd say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we break now for 25 minutes. We'll resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, before we recessed, we were looking at 65 ter 00742. I'd like to direct your attention to three entries in that exhibit. So, first is down to page 2 of the English, page 4 of the B/C/S. The page on the screen now refers to the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Bratunac. And if we turn to page 2, that's a reflection of the minutes of the first Serbian Assembly held on 30 December 1991. If we could turn to page 3, then, of the English, page 6 of the B/C/S. Which reflect the minutes of the first regular session of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Bratunac held at 1700 hours on 13 February 1992. And finally if we could turn to page 6 of the English, page 10 of the B/C/S, which reflect the minutes from the meeting of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Bratunac held starting at 1900 hours on 28 February 1992. Mr. Gusic, do these meetings in this document -- is this consistent with -- sorry, we just want to correct. That was page 9 of the B/C/S. I don't know if the witness had a chance to see the date of February 28. Thank you. Mr. Gusic, I simply wanted to ask you whether these entries are consistent with your understanding at the time of the establishment of parallel structures by the SDS in Bratunac municipality, including a separate Assembly.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender those entries, Mr. President. I believe that's 1 through -- I can work it out with the registrar. I think that's 1 through 7 of the English and about 2 through 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, you also referred in your statement and of course today to aspects of the relationship between the Bratunac SDS and the republic level, in particular, Mr. Karadzic. If I could turn your attention to three entries from 65 ter 00590. The first at page 53 of the English and page 42 of the B/C/S. These are the minutes of the 11th session of the Municipal Board held on December 17, 1990. And if could I direct your attention to the bottom of the page in English, and this page and the next page in B/C/S, which states after -- after a quick listing of what some people said indicates that the board accepted our agreement with one vote against it by a certain individual who disagreed with it. If the SDA rejects this variant as well, the board concluded that our Main Board should urgently be informed about everything. And then if I could next turn your attention to page 68 of the English and page 58 of the B/C/S. These are the minutes of the 15th session, so four sessions later, as we discussed, of the Municipal Board of the SDS of Bratunac. As we discussed before, this is indicated as the date of February 21st, 1990, but I think contextually it appears to be 1991 after the session we just looked at, and if you look at the first entry -- could we have the next page in B/C/S, please. And if you look at the first entry after the list of the agenda items following point 1, Mr. Deronjic, President of the Municipal Board, informed and communicated the information to the board. He informed the board about all opinions of the president of the party as well as of the leadership of the party regarding the declaration by the SDA and that is where the opinion of the party is negative. Finally if I could turn your attention next to page 74 of the English and page 63 of the B/C/S. This is the 17th session of the Municipal Board of the SDS of Bratunac held on April 12th, 1991. And if we go to the next page in B/C/S and look toward the bottom of the page in English. Following a discussion of regional redrawing of Municipal borders which is being carried out in Banja Luka, et cetera, the reference that our Presidency should urgently meet with Karadzic following all those questions. Mr. Gusic, I wanted to ask you whether these references to informing the Main Board, advising of the opinions of Karadzic, meeting with Karadzic and so on are consistent with your understanding of the hierarchical link and contacts with the republic level by the Bratunac SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask something. I wonder, would it be a good idea if Mr. Tieger could tell us whether this witness attended these meetings and whether he's best placed to comment on the meetings of the SDS if he did not attend them. At that time, after all, they were his political opponents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it would be better to discuss it with someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your intervention is not proper at the moment. It's clear from the -- Mr. Tieger's question what he's asking the witness to answer. Your points can be explored during your cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, if you remember the question, it was whether these references, and I summarised some of them, are consistent with your understanding of the contacts between the republic level and the Bratunac SDS and the hierarchical link -- the hierarchical relationship.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: They are. They are completely consistent with what I've been saying about the links between the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party and its president, Deronjic, and President Karadzic at the helm of the top leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender the -- those documents, Your Honour, reflecting those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those will be again added to Exhibit P3197.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic -- can we call up 65 ter 30190. Mr. -- while that's being called up, Mr. Gusic, you referred in your amalgamated statement at page 19 to an event in Kravica in which two Muslims were killed and two wounded and you further explained in your statement about the arrival of republic level officials including Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Ganic. I'd ask you to look at this document which is a conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and Radovan Karadzic on the 4th of September, 1991. And if you could look in particular toward the bottom of the page in both versions where it states: "Did you know that shots were fired up in. "I heard two dead weren't there. "Three. I think the third one's dead. Two are seriously injured. And Krajisnik says, "all Muslims." Karadzic: "All Muslims, but they attacked the Serbian village of Kravica." Krajisnik: "I'm not sure if that's true. You know what I said this morning, please?" Karadzic: "Yes?" Krajisnik: "Cengic called me." And it goes on. Have you seen that document before, Mr. Gusic. Are these references to the incident at Kravica that you described in your -- or that you discussed in your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's the same date and the same action.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd ask that to be MFI'd, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P3200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Gusic -- if we could call up Mr. Registrar 65 ter 07028. Mr. Gusic, you spoke at page 10 of your statement about the removal of weapons from the local depot or arsenal removal by the JNA and placing them under JNA control. If I could ask you to look at this document which is dated 14 May 1990. It's from General Adzic, and it's a document of the Federal Secretariat For National Defence, Main Staff of the SFRJ Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it is an order in order to provide the safe storage and safe-keeping of the Territorial Defence weapons and ammunition and in keeping with the tasks laid out by the federal secretary. And then it refers to organising the takeover storage and safekeeping of the complete stock of the TO weapons and ammunition in the JNA supply dumps and so on. Item 2 refers to: They should be stored and safe-guarded in TO depots guarded by JNA units. The TO staffs and TO units are to take out weapons and ammunition required for the execution of planned activities with the approval of the military district commands and so on. Mr. Gusic, is this document a reflection of or consistent with the removal of the weaponry and controlling them by the JNA that you spoke about in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document, and it's consistent with what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you're tendering associate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be all admitted. Shall we give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 11734 will be Exhibit P3203. 65 ter number 11733 will be Exhibit P3204, and 65 ter number 00749 will be Exhibit P3205.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Excellencies. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before I begin, I would like to address the Chamber for a few minutes with your leave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness is simultaneously a witness and a participant in important events. His statement contains 78 paragraphs. There are many paragraphs and many statements from other statements that are of interest to me. There are many general statements that he repeated earlier today and many documents. I have less than half a minute per item. If we take into account 78 paragraphs and everything else that's important, I have less time than I need even to phrase a question. Yesterday, I omitted a lot. I did not have time to proffer the judgement that convicted the witness to ten years' imprisonment, and I didn't have time for many articles from the media and many other things, and I will have to deal with it through a bar table motion, including the judgement convicting the witness to ten years' in prison. But what's important to me today and what was important with the witness yesterday was the question of their credibility. Please take into account the time limitations and this rhythm that is lethal. You see how many things Mr. Tieger is introducing through this witness that the witness is not even aware of, things discussed at meetings that he didn't attend. Please consider the possibility of at least giving me the whole day today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in reaching the conclusion as to how much time you should have for your cross-examination with a specific witness, the Chamber considers all the relevant matters, taking into account a number of factors including the nature and the -- the scope of the witness's testimony, the amount of the -- or volume of the witness's 92 ter evidence, the number of documents the Prosecution is going to use with a witness, the time estimate for the Prosecution's cross -- examination-in-chief, as well as your request. I do not agree with you that you haven't had enough time to cross-examine the witnesses. This is particularly so in light of the fact that you have spent much of your time on exploring irrelevant or marginally relevant issues. As emphasised several times before, you need to focus your cross-examination on important issues and make your best point first. Indeed, some witnesses may make general statements, but that does not mean that you should explore every single general statement a witness may make. The point of cross-examination is to pick certain parts of evidence led in chief that can be challenged. Again, I say again that you should focus on challenging the evidence of the witness in certain areas, preferably where you have best material to do so. So I would like you to refrain from making these statements about you being disadvantaged by having a short time. Let us move on. The Chamber at this moment is not minded to extend the time allowed to you at the moment. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There's just one more thing I have to say. It would be easy for me to follow your instructions if that would mean that what I did not have time to challenge cannot constitute a basis for a conviction. I cannot make a selection if anything that I do not deal with will serve as a basis for a conviction. That is how all my predecessors defended themselves, and I know that many innocent men were convicted and found guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is an improper comment at the moment. I would like you to consult your legal advisor how to conduct your cross-examination in a limited time which in the opinion of the Chamber is sufficient for your cross-examination. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to remind you of one more thing. The Prosecution used more time that they had originally said they would be using, so please reconsider that as well, and I conclude on that note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, do you know that I negotiated with Mr. Izetbegovic, rarely with Mr. Cengic, and never with Mr. Brka?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have been informed that you talked and negotiated with Mr. Izetbegovic and his associates. As for Brka, I came here to testify, to state the facts. Since I learned only later from Brka that he did not discuss that subject with you, I made that correction. Brka said to me, "I'm not sure that I talked to Karadzic." It was Kalinic. Perhaps you didn't understand me sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, whenever I put a specific question, yes or no answers will do. Did you know that the first man who presented the idea on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina was Mr. Izetbegovic and that he presented that idea to us at a meeting in order to persuade us to agree to the secession of Bosnia? You can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Did you know that the idea of the cantonisation of Bosnia was first launched by Vecernji List, a daily in Zagreb, and the first Serb reaction was by Professor Plavsic? She said that it was an interesting idea and should be looked into. All of that was in the media.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you commit a war crime during this war?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: No, did I not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you on lists of potential war criminals that should be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: When I testified in the Milosevic case, that was the first time that I found out that I have purportedly been accused of war crimes and there is a certain publication in the institutions of Republika Srpska. I told him then that it was the first time I heard of it. As for myself, no legal organ of Republika Srpska never informed me officially, either in writing or orally, that I was on some list or that there is any kind of criminal complaint. That is something I saw in the media later. In addition to myself, there are about 3.000 other Bosniak Muslims against whom similar criminal reports were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are among these 3.000 that are suspects; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I can only speak for myself. I saw what is written there, and that is pure fabrication. It has nothing do did with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of speed, I'm now just going to put to you what I know, what I found out about how things developed, and it will be sufficient for you to say that you agree or disagree. Later on when we display documents, we may discuss this in greater detail. Is it correct that the president of the municipality was the number one man of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipality in 1991 and 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 1990, after the elections.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: After the elections. In a way, yes. The president of the municipality and the President of the Executive Board, those were two parallel positions as it were in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the president of the municipality was not more important than the President of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. I'm just saying that these two positions were parallel positions as far as the municipality of Bratunac was concerned and when these positions were being allocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the chief of the public security station and the commander of the public security station? Are these two parallel positions as well when there was this power sharing agreement?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps they are not parallel. They don't have the same weight, the chief and the commander as far as powers and authorities are concerned, tasks and responsibilities, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I put to you: That the president of the municipality is more important than the president of the executive board and that Nijaz Dubicic was president of the municipality and that the president of the executive was Rodoljub Djukanovic. The first one was a Muslim, the second one was a Serb, and also in the police, the chief of the public security station was Nesim Muratovic, a Muslim, and the commander of the public security station was Nikola Mandic, a Serb, and that these four -- that is regards these four positions, both of those that are more important went to the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: The Muslims did hold those positions but we should speak about the entire power-sharing arrangement at the time and the conditions that led to this kind of sharing. If you wish, I can speak at greater length. When things are taken out of context this way and when conclusions are made out of context it looks a bit different and basically things were a bit different than that. You know that we had the first multi-party elections and that at these elections the SDA won. Out of 60 seats in the Municipal Assembly, they had 31 or 51 per cent, then the Serb Democratic Party had 24 members of the Assembly or 40 per cent, and the other parties headed by SDP had 8 per cent of the vote. So in Bratunac there were 21.500 Bosniaks and 11.500 Serbs. There are 2 times more Bosniaks than Serbs however the outcome of the elections was far more in favour of the Bosniaks than of others because of the way in which the vote was carried out and because of the statute that was changed during the previous term of the previous municipality and when the results were known, when we looked at the old municipality of Bratunac, when allegedly they wanted to make their government official and to end on that note, the activists of the SDS managed to lobby the then Assemblymen to change the statute at the last session. Until then a simple majority was sufficient. This was rushed onto the agenda and then a two-third majority became a prerequisite so that is how the statute was changed. When we constituted the new Assembly after the first multi-party elections, there was this ultimatum from the SDS: Are we going to share power half/half, or are we simply not going to constitute an Assembly. We wanted to share power on the basis of the outcome of the elections 52/48 per cent. However, they did not agree to this kind of power sharing. They set a precondition. It's either going to be 50/50 or there will simply be no municipality of Bratunac municipal assembly that will be constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now correct something that is inaccurate in the examination-in-chief. It is not correct that you, the SDA, succumbed to pressures of the Serbs and the SDS to have a two-thirds majority introduced rather than a simple majority. Rather, it was the old Communist Municipal Assembly of the municipality of Bratunac that changed the statute; right?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: It was the old Assembly that changed the statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: But that was against the republican regulations that were in force at the time. We asked for that to be changed and to be brought into accord with republican regulations. I do apologise for speaking this way. We wanted to bring this in line with republican regulations. However, there was no will on the part of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why would there be any will on the part of the SDS when the statute was more favourable for them. However that statute was changed by the old socialist Communist Assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is just one of the inaccuracies there. Secondly, in terms of numbers, was it 50/50?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to this inaccuracy. I have to correct you. As you had put it, that is what I said and that is what my statement says, namely that it was the old Assembly that changed the statute. I don't see why that should be called an inaccuracy that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe Mr. Tieger interpreted you in such a way. When he was interpreting what you were saying, he said that you had succumbed to the SDS, namely that a two-third majority would be required. But that was done when the SDS was not in power. However, we clarified that. Now I'm asking you the following: In terms of the number of officials that were involved was the power sharing arrangement 50/50?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, you know how power's shared. You don't share everything immediately; you share certain positions. An agreement was reached then with regard to specify positions and that was divided on a 50/50 basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And within these four main offices or positions, two -- the two main ones were in the hands of the SDA and the two less important ones the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: We cannot single them out. We have to look at the entire package. If we look at the entire package, the President of the Municipality of Bratunac was a Muslim. The President of the Executive Board was a Serb. The chief of police was a Muslim. The police commander was a Serb. Also there was the Executive Board, that at the time had five positions. Three positions belonged to Serbs and two to Bosniaks. Later on we asked for a sixth position to be introduced so that it be balanced out to 3/3 and that is ultimately what was agreed upon. There was one more position in the Executive Board, and it was again 3/3. So if you look at the entire package, then it was a 50/50 power-sharing arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the way it was in the times of socialism that if the president of the municipality was a Muslim or a Serb that the President of the Executive Board would be from the ranks of the other ethnic community? Is this a good custom that existed irrespective of political system?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: You know full well that that is the way it functioned. One position would be given to one ethnic group and the other to another ethnic group and if there was a third one then they would get a third position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is clear that you and I know what we are talking about, but we are putting this to the Trial Chamber here. They are not familiar with our political system, and therefore we have to explain it to them. Mr. Gusic, I am going to tell you about what I know and what I learned about what happened in your environment, and you will just tell me whether you agree or not and then later on we're going to have a broader discussion, if necessary, on the basis of the documents that I'm going to show. So do you know that in Sarajevo on the 31st of March a decision was passed on the establishment of the Patriotic League and on the 30th of April it was actually established and Bratunac had a Municipal Staff and a unit of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: The 30th of March which year?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone. We can barely hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's impossible to follow at that speed. And why don't you ask questions one by one. Because of the overlap the interpreters were not able to hear you. So what was your answer as to the establishment of the Patriotic League in Sarajevo on 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is one of the results of the rush that I have to have and the second thing I've been saying is that this affects my health directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was do you know the SDA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please refrain from making inappropriate comments. So what was your answer to the establishment of the Patriotic League on 31st of March 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't remember that this was on the 30th of March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that this decision was carried out on the 30th of April and the Patriotic League was established on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that on the 10th or 11th of June the main political staff was established, the Council for the Defence of Muslims within the SDA in the police centre, Dom Milicija, and they remained as the political leadership of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's correct. I know that there were some meetings devoted to that topic, but whether that actually happened, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that Sefer Halilovic, until the end of September 1991, in 104 or 103 municipalities actually by the end of September 90 something and at the end of the year in 103 municipalities he established municipal staffs of the Patriotic League, regional staffs of the Patriotic League and units as well, detachments.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I simply cannot believe any such thing. Perhaps there was some mention of that. Perhaps there were some discussions to that effect or perhaps somebody wrote that on some piece of paper, but that something like that existed in practice in real life I really do not believe that. At least not in the area of the municipality of Bratunac where I was a local politician at the time on behalf of the SDA and part of the Executive Board. I was not in a position to go to all of these meetings I was not invited to all of these meetings but that does not mean that I don't know some things that I did not express interest at the time in certain developments that were underway. And as for this firm organisation of the Patriotic League, well, had that been the case, what happened in all these municipalities could not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are saying it was not a solid organisation, this Patriotic League, but it -- did it exist?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Maybe some people were daydreaming about it or trying to establish something on paper but I know that in Bratunac nothing like that happened in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the commander of the Territorial Defence after the first elections?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence after the first elections, I think it was Dzemo Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Of course he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to now present a picture of this peaceful Bratunac. Let us just go back to this document that was admitted a moment ago, Adzic's document. Is it the case that you were shown a document dated 14 May 1990 about the seizing of TO weapons and their placement in the JNA depot?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I was shown an order to remove those weapons. I think it was an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what kind of position I held on that date?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: 14 May 1990. I don't know about you, and I don't know if the SDS party was established at that time. Did you say May 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 14 May 1990, the order that you discussed concerning the removal of TO weapons signed by General Adzic.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know which position you held on 14 May 1990. I really don't know. I don't even know exactly when the SDS party was established, so how could I know which position you occupied at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not know about me on the 14 of May; correct? You had not heard of me at that point.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long ago that was? Twenty-one years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, the Serbian Democratic Party announced its establishment on the 3rd of July and was established, founded on the 12th of July, and this order dates back to two months before, and the Serbian Democratic Party did not contribute in any way to the removal of those weapons because it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Of course if it did not exist it could not have contributed, which doesn't mean that there had been no plans whatsoever to remove those weapons, some designs for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that or is this your speculation?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, based on everything that happened and looking back with the wisdom of hindsight, I think nothing happened by accident. Absolutely nothing happened by accident. And if you put together all the pieces of that mosaic, you can draw a conclusion -- draw some conclusions with a pretty great degree of certainty including that removal of TO weapons and putting them in a JNA depot. You see what's interesting here, try to make an analysis of which municipalities the JNA chose to remove TO weapons from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on 14 May 1990 the HDZ already existed in Croatia and Tudjman was already in power? It was back in April even?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know exactly which month or which year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of March, 1990, was the announcement made that the SDA would be established and it was established a bit later?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And on the 27th of March, 1990, Izetbegovic held a press conference announcing that it would be established.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I suppose it's so. If it was established in end May, it had to be announced a bit earlier. That sounds logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, were the plans of the nonexisting SDS the thing that made the JNA remove those weapons, or was it the plans of the already existing SDA that forced the JNA to react?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD GUSIC
utterances.text: You're asking me a leading question. You're trying to make me say something that would suit you, but I'm going to speak of things only as I see them and to try to substantiate what I'm saying. At that time we had certain information. There were certain people who were saying that Serbia, the Yugoslav People's Army, have great designs about creating Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have no time for political debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
